prompt: Use case: illustration-story. Asset type: a production atlas of circular illustrated tokens for Creation, an original elemental myth about making a vast living world. The reference is the APPROVED STYLE AND CONTINUITY anchor, not a sheet to copy unchanged. Paint new subjects in exactly that family: luminous opaque gouache, selective fine ink contours, strong simplified silhouettes readable at 64px; deep lapis interiors, jade and turquoise, burnt ochre, muted coral, warm ivory light, very narrow ivory-gold rims. Not glossy coins or flat generic pictograms. Each icon is a complete perfect CIRCLE with opaque painted interior and transparent empty space outside. Center each circle in its own equal grid cell, circle diameter 80 percent of the shorter cell side, generous empty gutters. Absolutely no letters, names, numbers, grid lines, labels, UI, watermark or cast shadows outside circles. No modern laboratory hardware, books, houses or buildings. Only the specified object inside each circle, with a simple dark ground or essential local context. Tiny details must not carry the meaning. Related states should differ in structure, not merely colour. Follow item order exactly, left to right, top to bottom. Exactly 20 circles in 5 columns and 4 rows. Landscape atlas. Exact cell subjects: CELL 1, Hunting mammals: Two lean furred predators with alert pointed ears, forward eyes and flexible tails move low through grass; the nearer one pauses with its muzzle close to the ground. Distinguish: Larger predatory body and stalking posture, without visible prey confrontation or vulnerable ancestor shelter. CELL 2, Predator and prey: A lean ochre mammal pursues a darker short-necked grazer across an open strip of grass, the prey turning away while the hunter extends forward. Keep clear space between them. Distinguish: Two different roles in an active pursuit, no gore and no diagram of broader nutrient connections. CELL 3, Dung: A small irregular dark-brown pile of herbivore dung rests in grass, with visible short plant fibers and a few flies kept too small to dominate. Distinguish: Discrete organic droppings above the ground, not a soil cross-section or a beetle rolling a ball. CELL 4, Dung beetles: One sturdy six-legged dark beetle pushes a round brown dung ball backward across ochre soil, its curved forelegs and hard wing cases clearly visible. Distinguish: Beetle-and-ball action is essential; no generic insect portrait or loose dung alone. CELL 5, Fertile grassland: Strong jade grass tufts rise above a dark soil cutaway where a beetle burrow and broken-down dung feed a fine pale root network. Distinguish: Grass growth visibly linked to waste burial beneath it, not generic green field or forest nutrient return. CELL 6, Food web: A compact grassland scene contains grass, a grazer, a lean hunter and a dung beetle, joined by broad unobtrusive ochre paths that return to the soil beneath the grass. Distinguish: Grassland feeding and nutrient relationships, not one chase, recovering woodland or a whole-world community map. CELL 7, Watering place: Two short-necked grazers drink at a shallow jade pool while a lean hunter remains partly concealed in distant grass; hoofprints mark the wet edge. Distinguish: Shared grassland water draws herd and predator, rather than isolated desert grove or protected refuge. CELL 8, Far-ranging birds: Three long-winged feathered birds fly above a sharp mountain saddle, their extended wings and differing distances forming one strong diagonal route. Distinguish: Feathered flock crossing mountain terrain; no phase cycle or insects. CELL 9, Seasonal journeys: Two small groups of feathered birds traverse a long pale looping route between a leafy warm branch and a snow-touched bare branch, with land and water below. Distinguish: Recurring bird journey between seasonal habitats; river migration uses walking mammals and one ground corridor. CELL 10, Island life: The established volcanic island now has a modest green canopy and two perched birds separated by a broad blue sea from a distant mainland edge. Distinguish: Living population isolated on the same island shape, without distinct call patterns or a bare cone. CELL 11, Different songs: Two related feathered birds perch on separate island branches across a strip of sea; one sends three short pale sound arcs and the other a longer rising pair. Distinguish: Bird calls differ across separated populations; no humans, music notation or suggestion that insects became birds. CELL 12, Many-voiced world: The hook-marked planet carries small distinct habitat patches at its rim: a forest bird, an island bird, a grazer and a canopy insect, each with a restrained outward ripple of sound. Distinguish: Whole pre-impact living world with several communities; no recovery stumps, ice margins or resurrected giants in later tokens. CELL 13, Impact winter: The recurring planet is wrapped in a dark ash-grey veil that blocks most sunlight, with a small fading impact scar at its rim and a cold bare strip of land below. Distinguish: Sun-obscuring impact aftermath rather than collision itself, glacier growth or a local fallen woodland. CELL 14, Deadwood refuge: The hollow underside of a fallen trunk shelters pale fungal threads, small invertebrates and two tiny pointed-nosed mammals, with damp dark ground protected beneath the wood. Distinguish: Habitat and decomposer food web dominate; the survivor icon gives the mammals central visual weight. CELL 15, Small survivors: The same pair of pointed-nosed, round-eared small mammals crouches in the sheltered hollow of a large broken trunk, with fungi nearby and an ash-grey clearing beyond the entrance. Distinguish: Recognizable ancestral mammals foregrounded in post-impact shelter, with no new unrelated body plan or cold-coat comparison. CELL 16, Seed cache: A shallow sheltered hollow beneath a log contains a tight cluster of intact ochre seeds; one familiar small mammal holds another seed at the entrance. Distinguish: Deliberately gathered store with an animal custodian, not a loose seed sample or dispersed trail. CELL 17, Green shoots: Four tiny vivid jade shoots break through ash-grey soil beside a broken black branch, each emerging from a partly visible surviving seed. Distinguish: Multiple new shoots in damaged ground; no tall saplings, moss carpet or isolated clean germination diagram. CELL 18, Returning pollinators: Two clearly six-legged flying insects visit coral flowers on young saplings beside an old broken trunk; the small green canopy remains open. Distinguish: Returning insect population in recovery woodland, not a close pollen-transfer diagram or fruit-bearing branch. CELL 19, Returning fruit: A young jade sapling beside a dark old stump bears a few plump coral fruits, one split enough to show seeds; a pollinating insect is small and secondary. Distinguish: Fruit attached to young recovery growth with old damage retained, rather than an isolated ripe branch. CELL 20, Spreading mammals: Three related furred mammals spread from a deadwood shelter into young woodland: a small pointed-nosed ancestor, a sturdier ground browser and a nimble branch-climber. Maintain shared ears, fur and four-limbed anatomy. Distinguish: Diversifying descendants of established small mammals across habitats, without suggesting their first origin after impact. Keep the common circle size and painted finish. Anatomical lineages matter: insects have six legs, birds feathered wings, bats membranous finger-supported wings. A depicted early cell is a symbolic magnified view, not a modern laboratory slide. The world is not Earth's recognizable map. People, if listed, have varied warm earth-brown complexions, simplified features and no modern objects. Never add people, plants or animals to a subject that predates them. Do not draw the subject names.
